extracted.intended_audience: aspiring short-fiction writers and readers curious about magazine submission/editing practices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and editorial perspective on how magazines handle submissions, solicitation, and how new authors can approach submitting short fiction to periodicals. Focused on magazine editorial policy and practical advice for writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-solicitation policy (Clarkesworld)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarkesworld does not solicit submissions; authors sometimes encouraged to submit but are never given any advantage over other submitted works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gathering and reviewing submissions is part of the job and the editor wants it to be as open as possible. The magazine casts the widest net to find the best stories and therefore avoids solicitation or backroom dealing, even with authors previously published by the magazine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open submissions and 'clean slate' treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors will not hold previously submitted works against you; each submission is treated on its own merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors often look back at prior submissions to check for mistakes, but they do not permanently penalize authors for past rejections. Authors should keep submitting and improving; persistence is common among new authors who eventually get published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement for international submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should encourage writers from other parts of the world to submit to break the perception that the US market is closed to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively submitting to US magazines can help international authors overcome the belief they are unwelcome — editors may explicitly encourage such submissions to widen the pool of talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicited work does not guarantee best quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Soliciting stories doesn’t guarantee the best work; solicited authors are capable but solicitation is a gamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors who solicit may get capable work, but that practice doesn’t ensure superior stories. Magazines that avoid solicitation believe casting a wider net yields better discovery of high-quality pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazines rely on subscriber trust, shaping solicitation behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines depend on subscriptions and subscribers generally trust the editor and the magazine’s track record rather than knowing content in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because subscribers buy based on faith in the editor’s selections, magazines often avoid solicitation; reputation and trust both drive submissions and the presence of name authors even without soliciting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation is more common in anthologies than magazines
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthologies frequently solicit authors because a one-off book benefits from name authors who help sell copies; magazines rarely do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An anthology’s sales depend on the single volume, so soliciting known names increases marketability. Magazines, which rely on ongoing subscription revenue, have different incentives and so solicit less.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation used as a targeted tool (translations, Kickstarter, new-magazine launch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets solicit occasionally to fill specific needs—e.g., translations, Kickstarter marketing, or to highlight the kind of work a new magazine wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Future Science Fiction solicits translations to fill specific gaps; Uncanny and others solicit for Kickstarter campaign marketing; new magazines sometimes solicit to establish a desired tone or showcase examples when launching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Big houses vs. small press practices for anthologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-call anthologies are fairly unusual at bigger publishing houses; the small press produces the majority of anthologies and may operate differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers looking for anthology opportunities should note that small presses are more likely to run open calls, whereas big publishers often use solicitation for anthology projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence and improvement as key author attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors Clarkesworld has published who were new kept submitting and improving their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not self-reject; keep writing and submitting. The editor notes publishing a new author is a joy and that there are more opportunities now than in past — but success typically follows repeated submissions and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation is an exception, not the norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Although solicitation exists in the market, it is considerably less widespread than some believe, and even publications that solicit usually still accept from open submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should be aware of exceptions but not assume solicitation blocks access to magazines broadly. While it may limit some high-profile slots, overall opportunities for new authors remain and solicited authors often experienced similar early-career barriers themselves.
